questions: What does RTO (Recovery Time Objective) define?
The maximum acceptable time to restore a service after a disruption
The maximum acceptable amount of data loss measured in time
The time taken to back up a database

Recovery Time Objective (RTO) is the maximum tolerable time between a disruption and restoration of the service. It drives choices such as automated failover, warm standby or active/active. Recovery Point Objective (RPO) is the maximum tolerable data loss measured in time, which drives replication mode and backup frequency. They are independent: a service can have a short RTO and a long RPO, or the reverse.
The payment API has an RTO of 15 minutes: it must be back within 15 minutes of an outage.
RTO = how long down. RPO = how much data lost.
What does RPO (Recovery Point Objective) define?
The maximum acceptable amount of data loss, expressed as a period of time before the failure
An RPO of 0 means no data loss (requires synchronous replication). An RPO of 5 minutes means losing up to 5 minutes of data is acceptable, which allows asynchronous replication or frequent backups.
An event analytics platform accepts an RPO of 1 hour; the payment ledger needs an RPO near 0.
RPO 0 -> synchronous replication. RPO above 0 -> asynchronous replication or backups.
What is the difference between high availability (HA) and disaster recovery (DR)?
HA keeps a service running through local failures (pod, node, zone) automatically; DR restores service after a site- or region-wide disaster, often in another location
DR handles pod failures and HA handles regional failures
HA requires backups; DR does not
HA uses redundancy within a site or region with automatic failover. DR covers large-scale loss and usually involves a second site, replication or backups, and a failover process.
Correct: local resilience versus site or region recovery.
Wrong: DR relies on backups or replication.
Native HA across 3 zones is HA; replication to another region is DR.
Exam trap: zone-redundant HA does not equal regional DR.
A business states that its order integration can be unavailable for at most 1 hour and can lose at most 5 minutes of orders. Which statement is correct?

Downtime tolerance maps to RTO: the service must be back within 1 hour, which bounds the failover or restore procedure. Data-loss tolerance maps to RPO: losing at most 5 minutes of orders bounds the replication lag or backup interval. Translating business statements into RTO and RPO is the first step of any resilience design.
The DR design uses asynchronous replication with lag under 5 minutes and a 45-minute failover runbook.
Translate business statements into RTO and RPO first.
Which DR strategy generally gives the LOWEST RTO?
Active/active across sites, with traffic served from both
Backup and restore to a newly built cluster
Cold standby with no running infrastructure
Pilot light with only data replication
Active/active already serves traffic in both sites, so recovery is near instant. Backup and restore, and cold standby, take longest; pilot light and warm standby sit in between.
Correct: active/active gives the fastest recovery.
Wrong: faster than cold, slower than active/active.
The API layer runs active/active in two regions behind global load balancing.
Lower RTO and RPO means more cost and complexity.
A company wants active/active across two regions for a CP4I solution that uses APIs, ACE, MQ and Kafka. Which statement is MOST accurate?

Stateless tiers (gateways, ACE runtimes) can be active/active easily; stateful messaging needs careful design, for example region-local queue managers with routing or ownership of messages per region, Kafka topics per region with MirrorMaker 2, and idempotent consumers, because a single queue or partition cannot be actively written in two regions with synchronous consistency
Everything can be active/active by simply deploying twice
Stretch one queue manager across regions
Kafka provides synchronous multi-region writes by default
Active/active for stateful components requires data partitioning by region and asynchronous replication with conflict-free designs. Stateless layers are straightforward.
EU orders are owned by the EU queue managers and US orders by the US queue managers; events are mirrored across regions for global analytics.
Active/active stateful design = ownership and partitioning + asynchronous replication + idempotency.
Adding more instances (replicas) of a component to share load
Giving one instance more CPU and memory

Horizontal scaling (scale out) adds more instances, such as replicas behind a Service. It suits stateless components and improves availability as well as capacity. Vertical scaling (scale up) gives an existing instance more CPU or memory. It suits components with a single active writer, such as one queue manager, but is bounded by node size and often needs a restart.
ACE runtime replicas go from 2 to 6 during peak hours.
Stateless -> scale horizontally. Single-writer stateful -> often scale vertically.
Increasing the CPU and memory resources allocated to an existing instance
Vertical scaling raises the resources of an instance. It is useful when a component cannot be split, such as a single active queue manager.
A Native HA queue manager's CPU limit is increased from 2 to 4 cores to handle more persistent messages.
A queue manager has one active instance, so vertical scaling or more queue managers adds capacity.
A single Native HA queue manager is at maximum CPU. Which is a valid way to scale MQ capacity beyond one queue manager?
Add more queue managers (for example a uniform cluster) and distribute applications across them
Increase Native HA replicas to 10 so all are active
Add more consumers to the replica pods
Native HA has one active instance; replicas are standbys. Throughput scales beyond one queue manager by adding queue managers, for example in a uniform cluster with application rebalancing.
Correct: scale out with more queue managers.
Wrong: replicas do not serve applications.
Four uniform cluster queue managers each handle a quarter of the application instances.
Native HA replicas give availability, not throughput.
Which ACE workloads scale BEST horizontally?
Stateless HTTP or MQ-driven flows where any replica can process any message
Flows relying on in-memory state shared between requests
Flows requiring strict global ordering on one queue
Flows writing to a local file used by later requests
Stateless flows scale with replicas. State in memory or local files and global ordering requirements limit horizontal scaling.
Wrong: replicas do not share memory.
Wrong: replicas do not share local files.
An HTTP enrichment API scales from 3 to 9 replicas with no code changes.
Design for statelessness to unlock elasticity.
What does the HorizontalPodAutoscaler require to scale on CPU utilization percentages?
CPU requests defined on the pod's containers, and the metrics API available
HPA calculates utilization as usage divided by the request. Without requests, percentage-based scaling cannot work.
Wrong: utilization is based on requests.
An HPA targeting 70% of a 500m request scales at an average of about 350m.
HPA 'unknown' metrics -> missing requests or metrics server.
An HPA shows TARGETS '<unknown>/70%' and never scales. What is the MOST likely cause?
The pods have no CPU requests or the metrics are not available to the HPA
The deployment has too many replicas

The HorizontalPodAutoscaler computes utilization as current usage divided by the container's resource request. If pods have no CPU request, or the metrics API (metrics-server or Prometheus adapter) is not available, the HPA cannot calculate a value. It shows <unknown> and never scales. Define requests on every container that the HPA targets.
Adding resources.requests.cpu to the IntegrationRuntime template fixed the HPA.
HPA <unknown> -> check requests and the metrics pipeline.
An architect wants consumers to scale based on Kafka consumer lag rather than CPU. Which approach is appropriate?
Use event-driven autoscaling (for example the Custom Metrics Autoscaler / KEDA with a Kafka lag trigger), bounded by the partition count
Lag-based autoscaling reacts to backlog directly. KEDA (Custom Metrics Autoscaler on OpenShift) supports Kafka lag triggers, and the replica count should not exceed the partitions.
Consumers scale from 2 to 12 as lag exceeds 10,000 messages per partition.
Queue or lag-driven workloads -> KEDA triggers (Kafka lag, MQ queue depth).
An MQ-driven ACE flow must scale with queue depth, but scaling too aggressively overloads a downstream database. Which design is BEST?
Use queue-depth-based autoscaling (for example KEDA with an MQ trigger) with a maximum replica cap and additional-instance limits sized to the database's capacity, plus monitoring of database latency
Unlimited autoscaling to clear the queue as fast as possible
No autoscaling and a single replica forever
Scale based on API Connect analytics
Autoscaling should respect downstream limits. Capping replicas and concurrency protects the database while still reacting to backlog, which is better than either extreme.
Correct: demand-driven scaling with protective caps.
maxReplicaCount 6 keeps database connections under 120 while clearing peak backlogs within 10 minutes.
Scale to the slowest dependency's capacity, not just to the backlog.
What scales the number of worker NODES in OpenShift when pods cannot be scheduled due to insufficient resources?
The ClusterAutoscaler, together with MachineAutoscalers on MachineSets

Pod-level and node-level autoscaling are separate. The HPA changes replica counts. When new pods cannot be scheduled for lack of capacity, the ClusterAutoscaler (with MachineAutoscalers attached to MachineSets) adds worker nodes, within configured minimum and maximum limits, and removes underused nodes later.
A spike causes Pending pods; the autoscaler adds two workers in 6 minutes.
Two levels: pod autoscaling and node autoscaling.
An HPA scales an ACE runtime up and down every few minutes (flapping), causing constant pod churn. What should be adjusted?
The HPA behaviour settings (stabilization windows and scale-down policies) and, possibly, the target utilization, to smooth scaling decisions
Delete the HPA and the deployment
Set the CPU limit to zero
HPA v2 behaviour settings allow scale-down stabilization windows and rate policies that prevent oscillation.
A 300-second scale-down stabilization window stopped the flapping.
How does a Kubernetes Service distribute traffic to pods by default?
It load-balances connections across ready endpoints (pods) selected by the Service
It sends all traffic to the oldest pod
It sends traffic only to pods on the control plane
It duplicates every request to all pods
Services distribute connections across ready endpoints. Long-lived connections stay on one pod, which matters for MQ and Kafka clients.
HTTP requests to an ACE service spread across 4 replicas.
Connection-level balancing: long-lived connections do not rebalance automatically.
After scaling a set of MQ client applications, most connections land on one queue manager of a uniform cluster, which leaves others idle. Which MQ feature addresses this?
Uniform cluster application rebalancing, with clients using reconnectable connections and the same application name, so MQ redistributes instances across members
Uniform clusters monitor application instance distribution and ask clients to reconnect elsewhere to balance load. This requires reconnectable clients and consistent application identification.
After enabling reconnect and setting the application name, instances spread 3/3/3 across three queue managers.
Long-lived connections need active rebalancing, which uniform clusters provide.
How should external traffic be distributed across DataPower gateway replicas in CP4I?
Through the OpenShift router or an external load balancer to the gateway Service, which spreads requests across ready gateway pods
By hard-coding each pod IP in clients
Only to one pod with the others idle
Gateways sit behind Services and Routes or load balancers, which provide distribution and failover across replicas.
Three gateway pods receive traffic through the external IngressController shard.
Never couple clients to pod IPs.
Which TWO mechanisms provide traffic failover between two regions for API endpoints? (Select TWO.)
Global server load balancing (GSLB) or DNS-based failover with health checks
A cloud global load balancer or traffic manager routing to healthy regional endpoints
A Kubernetes Service spanning both clusters by default
Cross-region traffic management uses DNS or GSLB, or global load balancers, with health checks. Kubernetes Services are cluster-local.
Route 53 health checks fail over api.example.com from eu-west to eu-central within 60 seconds.
Cross-cluster traffic switching sits outside Kubernetes.
Why spread replicas of an API gateway across three availability zones?
So that losing one zone leaves the other replicas serving traffic

When replicas run in different availability zones, losing a whole zone (power, network or data center failure) removes only part of the capacity, and the remaining replicas keep serving. Spreading is enforced with topologySpreadConstraints or pod anti-affinity on the zone label, and works only if each zone has enough spare capacity.
With gateways in zones a, b and c, a zone A power outage reduces capacity by a third but causes no outage.
Plan capacity so the remaining zones can absorb the load.
A cluster spans three zones. Each zone runs at 80% utilization. One zone fails. What happens, and what should have been planned?

The remaining zones cannot absorb the failed zone's pods (they would need 120% capacity), so many pods stay Pending; capacity should be planned so that each zone runs at about 66% or less (N+1 by zone) for critical workloads
All pods move automatically with no impact
Surviving a zone loss requires spare capacity equal to one zone's load spread across the others. With 3 zones, utilization should stay at about two thirds or less for workloads that must fail over.
Wrong: requests are not reduced automatically.
After this lesson, the team keeps per-zone utilization under 60% and uses priority classes so critical pods schedule first.
Zone HA = replicas spread + spare capacity + priorities.
After a zone outage, Kafka partitions whose leaders were in the failed zone became briefly unavailable, then recovered. Producers with acks=all saw errors for some partitions longer than others. Why?
Partitions needed leader election from in-sync replicas in surviving zones; partitions whose ISR lacked enough replicas (below min.insync.replicas) refused acks=all writes until replicas caught up
Producers must restart for every election
Leader election is fast when in-sync replicas exist elsewhere. Writes need ISR at or above min ISR; partitions with shrunken ISRs reject acks=all writes until enough replicas are in sync.
Rack awareness (broker.rack set to zone) ensured each partition had replicas in three zones.
Enable rack or zone awareness so replicas spread across zones.
What does Kafka rack awareness (for example setting the rack to the zone label) achieve in Event Streams?
It spreads partition replicas across racks or zones, so one zone failure does not remove all replicas of a partition
It assigns consumers to zones only
Rack-aware replica assignment places replicas in different failure domains, which preserves availability during zone loss.
Wrong: that is a different feature (follower fetching).
The EventStreams CR sets rack topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/zone.
Zone-aware replica placement is essential for multi-zone Kafka.
What is API Connect two data center disaster recovery (2DCDR)?
An active/passive deployment of the management and portal subsystems across two data centers, with data replicated from the active to the passive site and a documented failover procedure
Two gateways in the same zone
2DCDR replicates management and portal data from the active to the passive data center. Gateways and analytics are deployed per site. Failover promotes the passive site.
Correct: active/passive replication of management and portal.
Management in DC1 (active) replicates to DC2 (passive); during DC1 loss, the operator changes DC2's multiSiteHA mode to active.
2DCDR = active/passive with replication. Know which subsystems it covers.
During an API Connect 2DCDR failover test, the passive site is promoted, but API calls in DC2 still fail. What should be checked?

That DC2 has its own gateway (and analytics) services registered and reachable, that DNS or GSLB points consumers to DC2's gateway endpoints, and that the catalogs are configured with gateway services available in DC2
That etcd in DC1 is running
2DCDR handles management and portal data. Runtime traffic requires gateways in the surviving site and traffic redirection. Failover runbooks must include both.
Correct: gateway availability and traffic routing.
Wrong: DC1 is down by definition.
The runbook now includes switching the GSLB to DC2 gateway endpoints after promoting management.
DR covers the control plane, data plane and traffic routing.
An organization uses MirrorMaker 2 to replicate topics from region A to region B for DR. During failover, consumers move to region B. Which considerations are MOST important?

Consumers must use translated offsets (checkpoints) or accept reprocessing; the replication lag defines the RPO; topic naming (for example a source prefix) must be handled in consumer configuration; and producers must be repointed and their ordering expectations understood
Consumers must always start from offset 0
Asynchronous mirroring means some data loss up to the lag and possible duplicates. Offset translation, naming conventions and producer repointing must be planned and tested.
Correct: offsets, lag (RPO), naming and producers.
Wrong: inefficient and causes heavy duplication.
Consumers in region B subscribe to regionA.orders using translated offsets; the runbook switches producers to region B's bootstrap.
Cross-cluster Kafka failover = offsets + lag + naming + producer switch.
Which is a common approach for MQ DR to another region when using queue managers in CP4I?

A replicated queue manager in the DR region (for example Native HA cross-region replication in supported MQ versions, or storage replication), with clients able to reconnect to DR addresses through CCDTs or DNS
An MQ cluster with the same queue name in both regions, assumed to replicate messages
Copying queue files nightly with oc cp
No DR is possible for MQ
MQ DR requires replicating queue manager data. MQ clusters distribute workload but do not replicate messages. Clients need a way to reach the DR queue manager.
Correct: replicated queue manager plus client redirection.
Wrong: clusters do not replicate messages.
Recovery group queue managers in the DR region receive asynchronous replication, and a CCDT lists both regional endpoints.
MQ DR = data replication + endpoint redirection.
What does OpenShift API for Data Protection (OADP) provide?
An operator based on Velero for backing up and restoring Kubernetes resources and persistent volume data (using CSI snapshots or file system backup) to object storage
OADP installs and manages Velero on OpenShift. It backs up namespaces and resources and volume data, and restores them to the same or another cluster.
A nightly schedule backs up the cp4i namespaces (CRs, Secrets, ConfigMaps) to S3.
OADP: Backup, Restore, Schedule CRs + DataProtectionApplication.
Which OADP resource defines recurring backups?

OADP is built on Velero. A Velero Schedule resource runs Backups on a cron expression and applies a TTL so old backups expire automatically. Backup performs a one-off backup and Restore restores one. The BackupStorageLocation defines where data goes; it does not trigger backups.
Schedule cp4i-nightly runs at 01:00 with a 30-day TTL.
Which TWO items are essential to back up so CP4I instances can be recreated on a new cluster? (Select TWO.)
Instance custom resources and their referenced configuration (ConfigMaps, Secrets such as certificates and credentials)
Persistent data, using each capability's supported method (for example queue manager data or API Connect database backups)
Recreating instances needs the declarative definitions and their secrets and configuration, plus the persistent state through product-supported backups.
Wrong: logs are not needed for restore.
Git holds the CRs, a vault holds secrets, and product backups hold the data, all tested quarterly.
GitOps covers configuration; backups cover state; both are needed.
An API Connect management restore to a new cluster fails to decrypt data. Which item was MOST likely not preserved from the original installation?
The management encryption secret (and the related certificates or secrets required by the documented restore procedure)
API Connect encrypts sensitive data in the management database. Restores require the same encryption secret and other documented secrets. Without them, the restored data is unusable.
Correct: the encryption secret is essential.
The DR runbook now stores the management encryption secret in the enterprise vault alongside backup locations.
Back up the keys that unlock the backups.
An OADP backup shows 'PartiallyFailed'. What should the administrator do FIRST?
Inspect the backup's logs and description (for example with velero describe backup --details) to find which resources or volumes failed and why
Ignore it because partial backups are fine
PartiallyFailed means some items failed, often volume snapshots or specific resources. The details identify them for remediation.
Wrong: risky; restore may be incomplete.
The details showed the CSI snapshot class missing for the cephfs volumes; adding it fixed subsequent backups.
Treat PartiallyFailed as Failed until explained.
Why must backup and restore procedures be tested regularly, not just configured?
Untested backups may be incomplete, incompatible with new versions, or missing keys; restore tests validate the RTO and RPO and the runbook
Testing is only needed once at installation
Restore tests reveal gaps such as missing secrets, version mismatches and storage class differences, and they measure the real RTO.
Correct: validation of recoverability and objectives.
A quarterly game day restores production backups into an isolated cluster and measures 2h10m against a 4h RTO.
'A backup is only as good as its last restore test.'
Which MQ items should be included in a configuration backup, separately from message data?
Queue manager object definitions and authority records (for example from dmpmqcfg) plus the MQSC and INI ConfigMaps and TLS key material
dmpmqcfg exports object definitions and authorities, so the queue manager configuration can be recreated. In CP4I, MQSC ConfigMaps and Secrets also hold configuration.
A nightly job stores dmpmqcfg output in Git for audit and DR.
MQ configuration is not messages. Back up both, by appropriate means.
After a database failover to a standby, ACE flows log connection errors for several minutes before recovering. What can reduce this impact?

Use a database endpoint that follows failover (virtual IP or DNS), configure connection retry and validation in the data source or policy, and ensure flows handle transient errors with retries or backout
Restart the cluster on each failover
Applications must reconnect to the new primary. Failover-aware endpoints, connection validation and retry logic shorten the impact.
Switching to the database listener's DNS name and enabling connection validation cut recovery from 8 minutes to 40 seconds.
Resilience is end to end: dependencies must fail over and clients must reconnect.
A DR test reveals that after regional failover, applications reconnect but process some messages twice. What should the architect recommend?
Design consumers to be idempotent (deduplicate by business key or message ID) because asynchronous replication and failover can cause redelivery; document the expected duplicate window
Make replication synchronous across continents regardless of latency
Duplicates are a normal consequence of at-least-once delivery and asynchronous DR. Idempotent processing makes them harmless.
Wrong: often impractical because of latency and availability impact.
The payment processor stores processed message IDs for 7 days and ignores repeats.
How many queue manager instances are active at any time in an MQ Native HA deployment of three replicas?

An MQ Native HA queue manager runs three pods. Exactly one is active and serves applications. The other two are replicas that receive the recovery log synchronously and stand ready to take over. A quorum (2 of 3) is needed to elect an active instance, which prevents split-brain.
qm-ibm-mq-1 is active; -0 and -2 are replicas.
How do client applications find the active instance of a Native HA queue manager in OpenShift?
Through the queue manager's Service or Route, which routes only to the active (ready) instance
By trying each pod IP manually
Only the active instance reports Ready, so the Service sends traffic to it. After failover, the new active becomes Ready and clients reconnect.
Correct: the Service routes to the active instance.
Clients connect to qm1-ibm-mq:1414, which always resolves to the active instance.
Readiness = active instance, which is how routing works.
A Native HA queue manager fails over often, and the logs show replicas falling behind and heartbeat timeouts. What is the MOST likely cause?
Network latency or packet loss between zones, or slow storage on replicas, which delays log replication and heartbeats
Use of TLS on application channels
Native HA relies on timely log replication and heartbeats between instances. Latency, packet loss or slow disks cause replicas to lag and trigger unnecessary failovers.
Correct: inter-instance network or storage performance.
Moving one replica off an overloaded node with a noisy neighbour stopped the spurious failovers.
Native HA needs low-latency networking and consistent disk performance.
What is the approximate failover behaviour of an MQ Native HA queue manager?
A replica with an up-to-date log is elected active within seconds and resumes service; in-flight uncommitted work is rolled back and clients reconnect
Failover takes hours because data is restored from backup
Messages committed on the old active are lost
Committed data is replicated to a quorum before acknowledgement, so the new active has it. Uncommitted units of work roll back, and reconnect-capable clients continue.
Correct: fast election with committed data preserved.
Failover takes about 10 seconds; JMS clients reconnect automatically and retry the rolled-back transactions.
Native HA protects committed data. Uncommitted work rolls back.
What is the minimum number of Kafka brokers recommended for a production topic with replication factor 3?
RF=3 requires at least 3 brokers to host 3 replicas on separate brokers. Spreading them across zones adds zone resilience.
Production Event Streams uses 3 brokers, one per zone, and grows to 6 as throughput rises.
RF must be no greater than the broker count.
A topic was created with replication factor 1 in production. A broker restarts and the topic's partitions on that broker become unavailable. What is the long-term fix?
Increase the topic's replication factor to 3 (through a partition reassignment) and enforce defaults so new topics use RF=3 and min.insync.replicas=2
With RF=1, each partition has a single copy, so any broker restart causes unavailability (and loss on disk failure). Reassign to RF=3 and set safe defaults.
Correct: increase RF and enforce defaults.
Wrong: avoids but does not fix.
Cluster defaults default.replication.factor=3 and min.insync.replicas=2 now apply to new topics.
How do you increase the number of ACE integration runtime pods in CP4I?
Increase spec.replicas in the IntegrationRuntime CR (or attach an HPA)
The replica count in the IntegrationRuntime CR controls horizontal scale, and an HPA can manage it dynamically.
Wrong: does not scale runtime pods.
replicas: 4 doubles the capacity of a 2-replica runtime.
An MQ-driven ACE flow needs more throughput but must keep the number of database connections low. Which approach is MOST appropriate?
Tune additional instances (threads) per runtime and the replica count together, sizing connection pools so total connections (replicas x pool size) stay within database limits
Set additional instances to 500 on every replica
Use one replica with one thread
Throughput comes from threads per pod times pods. Database connections scale the same way, so tune both deliberately.
Correct: balanced tuning of threads, replicas and pools.
3 replicas x 8 additional instances with a 10-connection pool = up to 30 database connections.
Concurrency multiplies across replicas. Calculate the totals.
Which deployment provides high availability for a DataPower API Gateway in CP4I?
Three or more gateway replicas spread across zones, with gateway peering for shared state, behind a load-balanced Service or Route
One gateway pod with a large CPU limit
Two gateway pods on the same node
A gateway with RWX storage only

DataPower gateway processing is largely stateless, so several replicas spread across zones behind a load-balanced Service provide availability and capacity. The small amount of shared state (rate-limit counters, token caches, subscription data) is kept consistent with gateway peering. A single replica is a single point of failure whatever its size or storage.
Wrong: a single point of failure.
Wrong: storage is not the HA mechanism.
The n3 profile deploys 3 gateway pods across 3 zones.
An odd number of peering members helps quorum-based peering operations.
Which element is MOST often missing from integration DR plans and causes failed DR tests?
Dependencies outside CP4I (DNS, certificates, identity providers, databases, firewalls, partner endpoints) that also need to be available or reconfigured in the DR site
DR often fails because of external dependencies: DNS records, certificates for DR hostnames, identity provider connectivity, firewall rules and partner allow-lists.
The DR test failed because the partner firewall allowed only the primary site's egress IP.
Map the full dependency chain for DR, beyond the cluster.
A documented, tested, step-by-step procedure (with owners and decision points) for failing over and failing back services

A DR runbook is a documented, rehearsed procedure: who declares a disaster, the exact failover steps per component, verification checks, communication, and the failback procedure. Under pressure, people follow the runbook rather than improvise, which makes recovery repeatable and measurable against RTO and RPO.
The runbook: declare the disaster, promote DR queue managers, switch GSLB, verify synthetic transactions, notify partners.
Include failback, which is often forgotten.
A pod of a 3-replica ACE deployment crashes. What does Kubernetes do automatically?
The ReplicaSet controller creates a replacement pod to restore the desired replica count, and the Service stops sending traffic to the failed pod

Kubernetes controllers continuously reconcile desired state. When a pod in a 3-replica Deployment fails, the ReplicaSet controller creates a replacement. Meanwhile the failed pod is no longer Ready, so the Service stops routing traffic to it. With multiple replicas, clients see no outage.
The crashed pod is replaced within seconds; clients see no errors thanks to the other replicas.
A node becomes NotReady. How long does it typically take before Kubernetes evicts and reschedules its pods (by default)?
After the default toleration period for not-ready or unreachable taints (about 5 minutes by default), unless pods specify shorter tolerations
Pods get default tolerations (tolerationSeconds 300) for node not-ready or unreachable taints. After that, they are evicted and rescheduled. This affects RTO for single-replica workloads.
A single-replica runtime was down for about 6 minutes after a node failure; adding replicas removed the impact.
Single replica = minutes of downtime on node failure.

An architect must design CP4I resilience for a payments platform with RTO 15 minutes and RPO near zero for payment messages, and RTO 4 hours with RPO 1 hour for analytics events. Which design is MOST appropriate?

Tier the design: payments on MQ Native HA across zones (RPO near zero within the region) with tested regional DR replication and automated failover steps; analytics on Event Streams with RF=3 in-region and asynchronous geo-replication or backups for DR; tested runbooks for each tier
The same backup-only strategy for everything
Active/active synchronous replication across continents for analytics
Single-zone deployment for both to reduce cost

Different services justify different resilience tiers. Payments need synchronous, quorum-based in-region HA and fast DR; analytics can use cheaper asynchronous options. Each tier's runbooks must be tested.
Correct: tiered resilience aligned to RTO and RPO.
Wrong: does not meet the payments RPO.
Wrong: does not meet the objectives.
The business impact analysis assigns Tier 1 to payments and Tier 3 to analytics, each with matching architecture patterns.
Match resilience investment to business criticality.
